transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sarah Patel (Orion Head of ML Ops), Dr. Kevin Burns (CTO), Alex Romero (Security Architect)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, terse):
- Customer evaluating on-prem / air-gapped deployment for PHI workloads (HIPAA).
- Primary concerns: offline update process, hardware inventory and constraints, KMS/HSM integration, auditability, performance on their GPUs and inference cost tradeoffs.
- Next steps agreed: send security pack, bench test plan, schedule pilot.

Topics: On-prem air-gap requirements; update/workflow; hardware checklist (GPUs, NICs); security and audit; timeline and pricing for pilot

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Really appreciate you making time. Quick intros, then Liam will walk through the private on-prem option and we can go into specifics.
[00:08] Sarah Patel: Hi Maya, Sarah here. We're mostly focused on keeping PHI inside our network and zero egress.
[00:12] Dr. Kevin Burns: Kevin, CTO. Short on time but want to make sure this fits our ops model.
[00:17] Alex Romero: Alex, security. I'll ask the hard questions, sorry in advance.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: Hi all, Liam from Redwood. I'll cover deployment model and the air-gapped update story.
[00:24] Maya Chen: Great. Liam, over to you.

[00:30] Liam O'Connor: Okay. So Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem installs and we also support fully air-gapped on-prem packages. The high level: we deliver a signed bundle that your infra team can pull into the isolated environment. All control plane APIs can be run locally, no outbound required.
[00:47] Alex Romero: When you say signed bundle, is that a container image or an appliance? How do we verify signature without internet root chain?
[00:54] Liam O'Connor: It's a signed tarball with container images and a signed manifest. We include an offline verification tool that verifies signatures against a root cert you install locally. The verification uses OpenSSL-based checks, so it doesn't need outbound.
[01:09] Sarah Patel: And updates? We can't have any automated outbound updates. Everything has to be manual push from our jump host.
[01:15] Liam O'Connor: Understood. We support a manual update workflow: you get a signed package on a USB or secure transfer, validate signatures, and then the private installer applies it. We also provide a reproducible RPM/DEB based installer if you prefer your package manager.
[01:30] Dr. Kevin Burns: What's the recommended cadence for model and runtime updates? Weekly? Monthly? And can we pin versions?
[01:36] Liam O'Connor: You can pin both runtime and model versions. For production PHI, customers usually do quarterly model updates and patch runtimes monthly, but it depends on your risk tolerance. Pilot can start with pinned model and runtime with a single allowed update path.
[01:49] Sarah Patel: We have a strict change window policy and a FedRAMP-ish internal process. We need full SBOM, provenance for binaries, and reproducible builds.
[01:57] Liam O'Connor: We can provide SBOM and signed build metadata. Our delivery also contains cryptographic hashes for each artifact.

[02:05] Alex Romero: What about KMS/HSM? We have an on-prem HSM cluster and want envelope encryption keys to never leave our HSM.
[02:13] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integrations. We have adapters for PKCS#11 HSMs and for common KMS APIs. The service can be configured to only use keys that live in your HSM; Redwood never sees plaintext keys.
[02:27] Alex Romero: Do you require a network egress for key checks?
[02:30] Liam O'Connor: No, the KMS calls are local to your environment. The adapter talks to your HSM endpoints inside the air-gapped network.

[02:36] Sarah Patel: Hardware — we don't have A100s in every rack. Our DC has a mix: two DGX racks with A100s, a handful of older V100s and some RTX A5000s for smaller workloads. We also have strict NIC constraints, 25GbE mostly.
[02:53] Liam O'Connor: That's common. We can run on mixed GPU fleets; the runtime prefers larger memory GPUs for larger context sizes, but we also support quantized runtimes for 16/8-bit models to fit on A5000 class. For throughput-sensitive endpoints you'd probably route heavier requests to the DGX racks.
[03:10] Dr. Kevin Burns: Do you support model quantization out of the box or do we have to produce quantized artifacts?
[03:14] Liam O'Connor: Redwood provides a quantized runtime and can ship quantized model artifacts as part of the bundle. If you prefer to quantize in-house, we support that too; just ensure the model format and ops are compatible.

[03:23] Sarah Patel: Latency vs cost is a factor. For triage workflows we need sub-200ms p50 on short prompts. For longer summarization it's okay to accept higher tail latency. What does Redwood recommend?
[03:36] Liam O'Connor: For sub-200ms p50 you'll need to ensure requests hit lower batch sizes and run on DGX/A100 with optimized kernels. For cost-sensitive batch jobs, we can recommend quantized smaller replicas and batching. We can provide a perf profile after we run the bench test.

[03:49] Maya Chen: Can you describe the bench test? What metrics will you measure?
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: We'll run a workload-shaped benchmark (your prompt types) and measure p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory utilization, and per-token cost estimates given our runtime. We'll also test cold starts and KV cache effectiveness.
[04:06] Sarah Patel: We'll share sample prompts and PII-scrubbed PHI examples.

[04:12] Alex Romero: Audit and logging — we need immutable audit logs, user-level tracing, and token-level redaction controls.
[04:20] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Private can be configured to write audit logs to your syslog/S3-compatible object store inside the air-gapped network. Logs can be signed; we also have a built-in redact tool to avoid storing raw prompt text if you want.
[04:32] Alex Romero: And RBAC? We use SAML SSO and internal groups.
[04:36] Liam O'Connor: We support SAML SSO and can map groups to RBAC roles. For full air-gap, the SAML idP can be inside your network. We also support local admin roles if needed.

[04:47] Dr. Kevin Burns: One of our concerns is model drift detection and quality monitoring. How does Redwood help with evals without sending data out?
[04:55] Liam O'Connor: You can run Redwood Optimize components locally. We provide an eval harness that runs your prompt sets and reports metrics locally. The alerts logic can be run inside your environment; you choose whether to export aggregated metrics out.
[05:08] Sarah Patel: Does that require additional licensing?
[05:11] Maya Chen: It can be included as part of the Private offering; we'll detail licensing in the SOW. For pilot we often include a reduced set for evaluation.

[05:19] Alex Romero: SLA and failover — if a rack fails, can the system fallback to another region or rack? In air-gapped setups region fallback may not be allowed.
[05:28] Liam O'Connor: For fully air-gapped, we're limited to within your DC. We support cross-rack redundancy and can orchestrate failover between racks in the same air-gapped network. For hybrid customers we can define fallback to Redwood Dedicated, but only if outbound is permitted and per policy.

[05:44] Sarah Patel: Compliance: HIPAA, SOC2 type II — do you have artifacts?
[05:48] Maya Chen: Yes, we have SOC2, ISO artifacts and a HIPAA-compliant offering. I'll send the security pack after the call.
[05:55] Alex Romero: We will need a BAA and evidence of penetration test schedule.
[05:59] Maya Chen: Noted, we'll include BAA template and pen-test summary.

[06:05] Dr. Kevin Burns: Pricing question — pilot cost and then scale. We'd like a 3-month pilot with limited throughput and a potential reserved commit after successful validation. What's typical?
[06:16] Maya Chen: Typical pilots are 3 months. For air-gapped pilots we charge for engineering setup and a pilot license which includes the private control plane and limited support hours. After pilot, customers often move to a reserved capacity model for predictable throughput. We'll include numbers in the SOW.

[06:30] Sarah Patel: Operational question: do we have to run your control plane processes, or can we run just the runtime and keep control plane offline?
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: The control plane can run locally; we provide a lightweight local control plane that manages routing, model selection, and observability. If you want to minimize surface area, we can run only the inference runtime and a minimal admin plane, but observability will be limited.

[06:53] Alex Romero: How is KV cache handled? Does KV cache persist across restarts and is it encrypted at rest?
[06:58] Liam O'Connor: KV cache persistence is configurable; it can be on encrypted local block devices and integrate with your KMS. We recommend encryption at rest and provide guidance for mounting with LUKS or vendor-specific disk encryption.

[07:12] Sarah Patel: For the bench we need to know supported model formats. We have internal Llama-derivative models and some third-party ones.
[07:20] Liam O'Connor: We support common formats: ONNX, GGUF, and model flavors we've ported. Llama-derivative models usually work; we may need to run a quick compatibility test.

[07:30] Dr. Kevin Burns: Will you be able to run the bench remotely or do you require an on-site visit?
[07:35] Liam O'Connor: We can run the bench remotely if you can provide SSH access to a jump host and the inventory; otherwise we can do a short on-site engagement. For air-gapped networks remote bench requires you to host the artifact and allow the SE to run tests inside the environment over an agreed window.

[07:52] Sarah Patel: Our change window is limited to weekends. That may affect schedule.
[07:56] Maya Chen: We'll coordinate with your ops calendar.

[08:00] Alex Romero: What about licensing for model weights? Some models have restricted licenses that may not allow distribution via third-party.
[08:08] Liam O'Connor: We can work with you on license compliance. For some third-party models we can provide a tooling path for you to ingest the weights directly so Redwood isn't redistributing them.

[08:20] Sarah Patel: Backup and restore — if we need to recover a model state or config, how do we handle backups inside air-gapped?
[08:27] Liam O'Connor: Backups are stored to your internal object store and we provide tooling to snapshot model stores and metadata. Restore procedures are documented and testable in your DR drills.

[08:38] Dr. Kevin Burns: Any known gotchas with multi-tenant racks and noisy neighbor problems?
[08:43] Liam O'Connor: We recommend dedicated GPU pools for high-priority production endpoints. Our scheduler supports GPU isolation and QoS to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

[08:55] Sarah Patel: We also need to validate export controls — encryption and key escrow policies.
[08:59] Alex Romero: Right, we can't have keys escrowed outside US boundaries, for example.
[09:04] Liam O'Connor: We can ensure keys never leave your boundary. Key escrow policies can be defined in the SOW.

[09:12] Maya Chen: Quick check — timeline? If we start pilot prep now when can it run?
[09:18] Sarah Patel: Earliest pilot window is late June given procurement and ops windows.
[09:22] Maya Chen: Okay, so bench week of 5/25 would be tight; maybe plan for engineering prep this week and bench in the first week of June or late June depending on ops.

[09:33] Liam O'Connor: We'll prepare the bench plan and hardware checklist. If you can share GPU inventory and network constraints by 5/18 that's helpful.

[09:40] Sarah Patel: We'll get that. Also Alex will share acceptable update procedure.
[09:44] Alex Romero: Yes I'll send the compliance matrix.

[09:47] Maya Chen: Anything else from your side?
[09:50] Dr. Kevin Burns: One more — SRE integration: do you expose prometheus metrics and tracing?
[09:55] Liam O'Connor: Yes, Prometheus-compatible metrics, Jaeger tracing hooks, and we can map metrics to your pager.

[10:03] Sarah Patel: Another tiny item: we need token-level cost accounting by route.
[10:08] Liam O'Connor: The private console includes token-level billing and per-route cost breakdown, similar to hosted. We can configure retention locally.

[10:18] Maya Chen: Perfect. I'll recap next steps. Liam, anything to add?
[10:22] Liam O'Connor: No, just that we'll include remediation steps for any perf issues found in the bench.

[10:26] Maya Chen: Recap and next steps: 1) Maya sends security pack + SOC2 artifacts and BAA template (due 5/14). 2) Liam sends bench test plan and hardware checklist (due 5/20). 3) Sarah provides DC GPU inventory (due 5/18). 4) Alex provides compliance/update matrix (due 5/17). 5) Schedule bench window with ops (target early June / late June pilot).
[10:46] Sarah Patel: Sounds good.
[10:48] Alex Romero: Yep.
[10:49] Dr. Kevin Burns: Thanks, we'll review and circle back.
[10:52] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up over email with the artifacts and a proposed SOW.
[10:57] Liam O'Connor: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
